blocks.content: The story starts where Two-Phase Commit left its biggest problem unsolved.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305053776-178540817.png
blocks.alt: 2PC blocking problem recap: coordinator crashes after YES votes, before COMMIT/ABORT

blocks.content: You have a distributed transaction. The coordinator sent PREPARE. All participants voted YES. They're sitting there holding database locks, WAL written to disk, waiting for the coordinator to say COMMIT. The coordinator crashes.
Now what? The participants cannot commit on their own what if one participant voted NO and the coordinator was about to send ABORT?
They cannot abort on their own what if the coordinator had already sent COMMIT to some other participant before crashing?
They have no way to know. So they wait. Holding locks. Blocking every other transaction that wants those rows. Until the coordinator comes back online.

This is the blocking problem of 2PC. Three-Phase Commit was designed specifically to solve it. It adds one more phase between PREPARE and COMMIT and that one phase changes everything about what participants can do when the coordinator disappears.
1. Why 2PC blocks
Before 3PC makes sense, you need to understand exactly which moment in 2PC causes the block. It's not just "coordinator crashes" it's the specific window.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130611-55988346.png
Why Window 2 Is Dangerous in 2PC
To understand the blocking problem in Two-Phase Commit (2PC), focus on what happens after all participants vote YES.

When a participant sends a YES vote, it is making a promise that it is ready to commit the transaction. At that point, it enters the prepared state, keeps its locks, and waits for the coordinator's final decision. It cannot independently decide what to do next.

The critical moment occurs after the coordinator has received YES from every participant but before the final decision is safely recorded and communicated. During this short window, the coordinator is the only component that knows the outcome of the transaction.

If the coordinator crashes at this moment, every participant is left in uncertainty. They know they voted YES, but they do not know whether the coordinator decided to commit or abort. They also do not know what decisions other participants received before the crash.

Because of this uncertainty, a participant cannot safely commit. Another participant may have voted NO, which would require the transaction to abort. At the same time, it cannot safely abort because the coordinator may have already committed the transaction elsewhere.

Since neither action is safe, participants must simply wait. They continue holding locks and remain stuck until the coordinator recovers and reveals the final decision. If recovery takes a long time, the locks remain held for a long time. If recovery never happens, the participants can remain blocked indefinitely.

This is the exact reason 2PC is called a blocking protocol. The problem is not that the coordinator crashes in general. The problem is that the coordinator crashes after everyone has voted YES but before the final decision becomes known to all participants.
During that brief period, the coordinator is the only source of truth, and when it disappears, the entire transaction becomes trapped in uncertainty.
2. The 3PC (Phase Commit)
3PC inserts a PRE-COMMIT phase between PREPARE and COMMIT. Before the coordinator tells anyone to commit, it first tells everyone: "I've decided to commit acknowledge that you know this."
Once a participant receives PRE-COMMIT and acknowledges, it knows:
["The coordinator decided to commit","All other participants voted YES (because PRE-COMMIT is only sent if all voted YES)"]
items: All other participants voted YES (because PRE-COMMIT is only sent if all voted YES)

blocks.content: Now if the coordinator dies, the participant is no longer uncertain. It knows the decision was commit. It can contact other participants to confirm they also received PRE-COMMIT, and then proceed to commit with or without the coordinator.
This is the breakthrough. The knowledge of the decision is no longer trapped in the coordinator's head.
Phase 1: PREPARE
The coordinator asks all participants:
"Can you commit this transaction?"

Each participant performs its local work, writes the information to disk, and sends either YES or NO. If even one participant sends NO, the coordinator immediately sends ABORT, and everyone rolls back the transaction. If everyone sends YES, the protocol moves to the next phase.
Phase 2: PRE-COMMIT
The coordinator now sends a PRE-COMMIT message. This means:
"Everyone agreed. We are going to commit."

Participants acknowledge this message by sending ACK. At this point, every participant knows that all nodes voted YES and that the transaction is moving toward commit. The uncertainty that existed in 2PC is removed.
Phase 3: COMMIT

After receiving ACKs from all participants, the coordinator sends COMMIT. Participants commit their changes locally, release any locks they are holding, and send a final acknowledgment. The transaction is now complete.
Why 3PC Adds PRE-COMMIT
In 2PC, after everyone votes YES, only the coordinator knows the final state. If the coordinator crashes, participants become stuck waiting.
3PC adds the PRE-COMMIT phase so that participants learn:
"Everyone has already agreed, and commit is the only possible next step."
Because participants have this extra knowledge, they can make progress even if the coordinator crashes later, reducing the blocking problem that exists in 2PC.
3. Participant states

In 2PC, a participant that voted YES has one state: prepared. Uncertain whether it will commit or abort. In 3PC, there's an additional state: pre-committed where the participant knows the decision is commit, even if the coordinator disappears.
1. 2PC Participant States
In Two-Phase Commit, a participant starts in the INIT state.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305057300-892166920.png
blocks.alt: 2PC participant state machine: INIT to PREPARED to COMMITTED or ABORTED

blocks.content: When the coordinator sends PREPARE, the participant checks whether it can successfully commit the transaction. If everything is valid, it writes the necessary information to disk, keeps its locks, sends a YES vote, and moves to the PREPARED state.
The PREPARED state is the problem.
At this point, the participant has promised that it is ready to commit, but it does not know the final decision yet. The coordinator might later decide COMMIT or ABORT.
Because the participant does not know the decision, it cannot commit on its own. It also cannot abort on its own because the coordinator may have already decided to commit elsewhere.
The participant is therefore stuck waiting.
If the coordinator eventually sends COMMIT, the participant moves from PREPARED to COMMITTED.
If the coordinator sends ABORT, the participant moves from PREPARED to ABORTED.

The problem occurs when the coordinator crashes while participants are in the PREPARED state. Since only the coordinator knows the final decision, participants may wait forever. This is the blocking problem of 2PC.
2. 3PC Participant States
Three-Phase Commit introduces an extra state called PRE-COMMITTED.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130611-466726720.png
A participant starts in INIT.
When it receives PREPARE, it performs the same checks as in 2PC. If everything is fine, it votes YES and moves to the PREPARED state. However, 3PC changes the meaning of this state.

If the participant stays in PREPARED for too long and does not hear from the coordinator, it can safely assume the transaction should abort and move to ABORTED after a timeout. It does not need to wait forever.
If the coordinator receives YES votes from everyone, it sends PRE-COMMIT. When a participant receives PRE-COMMIT, it enters the PRE-COMMITTED state.
This state is important because the participant now knows that:
Everyone voted YES and the system is moving toward commit.
The uncertainty is gone. If the coordinator later sends COMMIT, the participant commits normally.

Even if the coordinator crashes after PRE-COMMIT, participants already know that commit is the expected outcome. They can communicate with each other and eventually complete the commit process instead of remaining blocked forever.
4. What happens when the coordinator crashes: 3PC recovery
blocks.text: 4. What happens when the coordinator crashes: 3PC recovery

blocks.content: This is the critical part. 3PC's recovery protocol involves participants talking to each other when the coordinator goes silent. This is called the termination protocol.
Scenario A: Coordinator Crashes Before PRE-COMMIT
blocks.text: Scenario A: Coordinator Crashes Before PRE-COMMIT

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305058964-240455807.png
blocks.alt: Scenario A: coordinator crashes before PRE-COMMIT, participants abort safely

blocks.content: Everyone has voted YES and is in the PREPARED state, but the coordinator crashes before sending any PRE-COMMIT message.
The participants wait for some time. When the timeout expires, they communicate with each other and ask:
"Did anyone receive PRE-COMMIT?"
The answer is no.
This means the coordinator never announced that the transaction was moving toward commit. Since nobody has entered the PRE-COMMITTED state, aborting is still safe.
As a result, all participants abort the transaction and release their locks.
Scenario B: Coordinator Crashes After Sending Some PRE-COMMIT Messages
blocks.text: Scenario B: Coordinator Crashes After Sending Some PRE-COMMIT Messages

blocks.content: The coordinator successfully sends PRE-COMMIT to some participants but crashes before reaching everyone.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305060636-839343674.png
blocks.alt: Scenario B: coordinator crashes after some PRE-COMMIT sent, participants elect temp coordinator and commit

blocks.content: For example, participant A receives PRE-COMMIT, but participant B does not.
After a timeout, participants communicate with each other.
B asks:
"What state are you in?"
A replies:
"I am PRE-COMMITTED."
This changes everything.
PRE-COMMITTED means the system already passed the point where commit became the only valid direction. Someone knows the decision is commit.
The participants elect a temporary coordinator and finish the protocol themselves.
Everyone commits.
Scenario C: Coordinator Crashes After Sending COMMIT
blocks.text: Scenario C: Coordinator Crashes After Sending COMMIT

blocks.content: The coordinator sends COMMIT to some participants and then crashes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305062494-811327951.png
blocks.alt: Scenario C: coordinator crashes after some COMMIT sent, remaining participant commits

blocks.content: For example, participant A receives COMMIT and commits successfully. Participant B does not receive the COMMIT message before the crash.
After a timeout, participants communicate.
A reports:
"I already committed."
B reports:
"I am PRE-COMMITTED."
Since at least one participant has already committed, rolling back is impossible. The transaction has already become visible in the system.
Therefore B immediately commits as well.
No need to wait for the original coordinator to recover.
The termination protocol works on a simple rule: participants elect a new temporary coordinator among themselves. The new coordinator surveys everyone's state and applies this logic:

["If any participant is COMMITTED → everyone commits (someone already went through)","If any participant is PRE-COMMITTED → everyone commits (decision was commit, it's safe to finish)","If any participant is PREPARED → everyone aborts (PRE-COMMIT was never sent, abort is safe)","If any participant is ABORTED → everyone aborts (follows the original abort decision)"]
items: If any participant is COMMITTED → everyone commits (someone already went through)
If any participant is PRE-COMMITTED → everyone commits (decision was commit, it's safe to finish)
If any participant is PREPARED → everyone aborts (PRE-COMMIT was never sent, abort is safe)
If any participant is ABORTED → everyone aborts (follows the original abort decision)

blocks.content: This ruleset is what makes 3PC non-blocking under coordinator failure as long as participants can talk to each other.
5. Message count comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305064550-230921761.png
blocks.alt: Message count comparison overview: 2PC four exchanges versus 3PC six exchanges

blocks.content: Distributed commit protocols must exchange messages between the coordinator and participants to reach a consistent decision. The number of messages directly impacts network overhead and transaction latency.
2PC (Two-Phase Commit)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305066553-404580304.png
blocks.alt: 2PC message flow: PREPARE, YES/NO, COMMIT/ABORT, ACK

blocks.content: In 2PC, the coordinator first sends a PREPARE request to all participants. The participants reply with YES or NO. If everyone votes YES, the coordinator sends COMMIT; otherwise, it sends ABORT. Finally, participants send acknowledgements back to the coordinator.
For N participants, there are four message exchanges: PREPARE, YES/NO, COMMIT/ABORT, and ACK.

This gives a total of 4N messages. For example, with 3 participants, the total is 4 × 3 = 12 messages. Since there are two communication rounds, if each round trip takes about 1 ms, the coordination overhead is roughly 2 ms.
The advantage of 2PC is that it is simple and fast. The disadvantage is that participants can become blocked if the coordinator crashes at the wrong moment.
3PC (Three-Phase Commit)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305069761-615334481.png
blocks.alt: 3PC message flow: PREPARE, YES/NO, PRE-COMMIT, ACK, COMMIT, ACK

blocks.content: 3PC adds an extra PRE-COMMIT phase between voting and the final commit. After collecting YES votes from all participants, the coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT. Participants acknowledge it, after which the coordinator sends COMMIT and participants acknowledge again.
For N participants, there are six message exchanges: PREPARE, YES/NO, PRE-COMMIT, ACK, COMMIT, and ACK.

This gives a total of 6N messages. For example, with 3 participants, the total is 6 × 3 = 18 messages. Since there are three communication rounds, if each round trip takes about 1 ms, the coordination overhead is roughly 3 ms.

The advantage of 3PC is that it avoids the blocking problem by ensuring participants know enough to continue even if the coordinator fails. The trade-off is extra messages and slightly higher latency.
6. The Fatal Flaw

Here is why 3PC is almost never used in production despite solving the blocking problem. It assumes a fail-stop failure model nodes either work correctly or crash completely. In a real distributed system, the failure mode that matters most is a network partition where nodes are alive and running but cannot communicate with each other.
Under a network partition, 3PC's termination protocol can produce split-brain.
1. Partition A (Nodes 1 & 2)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027809-645210671.png
blocks.alt: Partition A: Nodes 1 and 2 isolated, no PRE-COMMIT seen, decide to ABORT

blocks.content: The coordinator crashes, and Nodes 1 and 2 become isolated from the rest of the system because of the network partition.
They communicate with each other and check the transaction state. Neither node has received a PRE-COMMIT message.
According to the 3PC rules, if no participant knows that the transaction was about to commit, the safest decision is to ABORT.
So Nodes 1 and 2 abort the transaction.
From their perspective, this decision is correct because they have no evidence that a commit was ever agreed upon.
2. Partition B (Nodes 3, 4 & 5)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305074261-239919621.png
blocks.alt: Partition B: Nodes 3, 4, 5 connected, Node 3 already PRE-COMMITTED, decide to COMMIT

blocks.content: The coordinator crashes, but Nodes 3, 4, and 5 can still communicate with each other.
Node 3 has already received the PRE-COMMIT message before the crash.
When the nodes exchange information, they discover that at least one participant reached the PRE-COMMIT state.
According to the 3PC rules, this means the transaction was very close to being committed, so they decide to COMMIT.
From their perspective, this decision is also correct because they have evidence that the coordinator intended to commit the transaction.
7. 2PC vs 3PC
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130611-394627107.png
8. What Replaced 3PC in Practice?
3PC solved the blocking problem of 2PC, but it introduced a bigger problem: data inconsistency during network partitions. Because of this, production systems rarely use 3PC.
Instead, modern systems use other approaches.
1. Highly Available Coordinator: Rather than adding another phase, modern systems make the coordinator highly available using protocols like Raft.
If one coordinator node fails, another node becomes the leader within milliseconds and continues the transaction. This is the approach used by systems like Spanner and CockroachDB.
2. Paxos Commit: Paxos Commit removes the dependency on a single coordinator. Participants use consensus to reach the commit decision.
This avoids blocking due to coordinator failure, but the protocol is much more complex.
3. Saga Pattern: Many distributed systems avoid distributed transactions completely. Each service commits its own local transaction and publishes an event.
If something goes wrong later, compensating actions are used to undo previous work.
This improves availability and simplifies the system.
4. Avoid Distributed Transactions: The most common solution is to redesign the system so related data stays in the same database.
Then a normal local transaction can handle everything without needing 2PC or 3PC.
9. Why 3PC Is Still Asked in Interviews
blocks.text: 9. Why 3PC Is Still Asked in Interviews

blocks.content: Interviewers usually don't care whether you would use 3PC in production. They want to know whether you understand the trade-offs.
1. What Problem Does 3PC Solve?
3PC adds a PRE-COMMIT phase before the final commit.
This allows participants to know that the transaction is about to commit, even if the coordinator crashes.
As a result, the protocol becomes non-blocking under coordinator failure.
2. Why Isn't It Used?
3PC assumes nodes either work correctly or crash completely.
Real systems also face network partitions, where nodes are alive but cannot communicate.
During a partition, one group of nodes may commit while another group aborts, leading to inconsistent data.
This is worse than 2PC blocking.
3. What Do Real Systems Use Instead?
blocks.text: 3. What Do Real Systems Use Instead?

blocks.content: Most systems use:
["2PC with a highly available Raft-backed coordinator.","Consensus-based approaches like Paxos Commit.","Saga Pattern for microservices.","Data models that avoid distributed transactions entirely."]
items: 2PC with a highly available Raft-backed coordinator.
Data models that avoid distributed transactions entirely.
